steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper arguing that static question-answer benchmarks overestimate LLM reasoning, proposing functional variants of benchmarks such as MATH and a 'reasoning gap' metric. Finish with a contributions subsection.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Reasoning evaluation matters; static benchmarks don't measure it well
- Contamination: novel questions are hard to guarantee
- Proposal: functional variants of benchmarks and the reasoning gap
- Which benchmarks can be functionalized
- Current status: functional MATH, results, future work
## 2.1 Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Reasoning evaluation
  - accurate evaluation critical to improving LLMs; current benchmarking fails to measure reasoning
  - accurate test: question whose answer is derivable from domain axioms; solvable without having seen it before
  - ideal: answer plus each derivation step (explicit steps ideal, not critical)
  - SOTA LMs have some reasoning, but evaluation lags; capabilities may be overestimated by benchmarks sufficient for language understanding (textual question, answer)
- Contamination
  - generalized problem-solving = answer unseen questions; opposite of knowledge retrieval
  - hard to find novel questions when trained on internet snapshot; offline datasets won't stay offline
  - k-contiguous token checks miss other leakage for static QAs:
    - i) paraphrasing / compressed representations / semantically similar fragments
    - ii) provenance of data at every training / fine-tuning stage, harder as models start from existing weights
    - iii) synthetic data from possibly contaminated model, esp. closed-source closed-data
    - iv) overfitting through preference tuning -> reinforcement feedback discovering correct static answers
  - static QA only an indirect test of reasoning: fine for humans, not for model outputs
- Proposal
  - works with existing evaluation harnesses
  - rewrite each static QA's reasoning into code; vary inputs -> infinite versions, same reasoning pattern, different steps
  - "functional variant"; running code -> snapshot, drop-in replacement in static harness
  - accuracy on replacements (with static included) may be lower than static alone = reasoning gap
  - Bench (MATH, GSM8K, HumanEval) -> Bench(rngs); QA(rngs) takes deterministic typed random generators rngs (natural int, positive/negative float, fractions, string, positive evens/odds, primes)
  - seeded rngs -> deterministic snapshot of each test (QA*) and whole benchmark
  - QA* differs from static QA but needs same reasoning
  - functionalization done manually for unbiased baseline; one-time, time-consuming; infinite snapshots
- Which benchmarks
  - easy: math (MATH, GSM8K), code (HumanEval, MBPP, Natural2Code)
  - not good candidates (test English understanding): commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag, Winogrande, PIQA, SIQA, OpenbookQA, ARC-Easy/Challenge, CommonsenseQA), world knowledge (NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA), reading comprehension (BoolQ, QuAC, DROP)
  - aggregated benchmarks (MMLU, HELM, BBH, AGI Eval): subparts could be functionalized
- Status
  - 41.2% of MATH functionalized; subset covers static QA tests solved by 4 closed-weight + 9 open-weight SOTA models
  - complete metrics over all of MATH for these models, simple few-shot prompting
  - reasoning gap 58.35% to 80.31%
  - gap with CoT, ToT, CoC etc. could be lower; open until 100% functionalized MATH()
  - future: GSM8K, HumanEval, MBPP

## 2.1 Contributions

- framework for evaluating models that have seen the whole internet: infinite snapshots, probabilistic guarantee of newness; QA* same process, new test; needs step-by-step derivation, not recall
- functional MATH + public snapshots: rework existing benchmarks without modification; functionalizing all of MATH; code never public; three snapshots every quarter; {Oct, Nov, Dec}-2023 at https://github.com/consequentai/fneval/ with eval code; kept up to date with last quarter

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Evaluating reasoning performance accurately is critical if we want to improve large language models (LLMs) beyond what they can do now. The current standard for benchmarking does not accurately measure the reasoning of LLMs. An accurate test should pose a question whose answer can be derived assuming the axioms of that domain. A reasoning system (or a human) should be able to reach the answer even if it has not seen the question before. Ideally the system would give not only the answer but also every step of the derivation. Explicitly spelling out the steps is ideal, but it is not critical. State-of-the-art language models show some reasoning capabilities, but accurate evaluation is lagging behind. In particular, the capabilities of LLMs may be overestimated, because they are tested with benchmarks that are sufficient for language understanding (textual question, answer) but that may not accurately measure reasoning.

When we test generalized problem-solving, the goal is to check whether the system can effectively answer questions it has not seen before. This is the opposite objective compared to knowledge retrieval. It is hard to find novel questions when the model was trained on a snapshot of the internet. Even if there are datasets that are not on the internet right now, it is unreasonable to expect that they will stay that way, or that we will keep developing novel datasets. Contamination testing that checks for k-contiguous token sequences does not account for many other ways leakage can happen, especially when the benchmark is a set of static text question-answers ("static QAs"). These include i) accidental leakage from paraphrasing or compressed representations in the training data, or fragments of semantically similar statements; ii) not tracking the provenance of the data used in every stage of training or fine-tuning, which gets more and more difficult as more models are trained starting from existing high-quality weights; iii) getting synthetic training data from an existing model that could be contaminated, especially if it is closed-source and closed-data; iv) overfitting through preference tuning, which in the extreme case may cause reinforcement feedback that lets the model evolve to discover correct static answers.

Checking against a static QA only tests reasoning indirectly. Text questions and answers work well for humans, since a correct answer implies that the stepwise reasoning was likely correct. This does not apply to model outputs.

We propose a different approach that reduces the concerns with static QA testing, and that also works seamlessly with existing evaluation harnesses. We propose to rewrite the reasoning of each static QA into code. The inputs of the code can be varied to create infinite versions that follow the same reasoning pattern, but the steps needed in each one would be different. We call this the functional variant of the benchmark. Running each of these code fragments creates a snapshot that is a drop-in replacement in the existing static evaluation harness. The accuracy on these replacements, with the static variant included, might be lower than the accuracy on the static variant alone, and we quantify this as the reasoning gap.

For domains where this is possible, using functional variants would improve on static QA evaluation. We would convert a static benchmark Bench (e.g., MATH or GSM8K or HumanEval) into its functional variant Bench(rngs). The functional variants (written here as QA(rngs)) take as input a set of deterministic typed random generators rngs, which output a pseudorandom typed value, e.g., natural int, positive or negative float, fractions, string, positive evens or odds, primes. When the rngs are seeded the instantiation is deterministic, and it generates a snapshot of each test (written here as QA*) and of the whole benchmark.

Each QA* text pair in the snapshot is different from the original static QA. But answering QA* needs the same reasoning as the static QA. To have an unbiased accurate baseline, we did the functionalization manually, by rewriting the reasoning of each test into code. Functionalization is a one-time, time-consuming task, and it gives infinite snapshot instantiations to test against.

- Which benchmarks
  - easy: math (MATH, GSM8K), code (HumanEval, MBPP, Natural2Code)
  - not good candidates, test English understanding: commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag, Winogrande, PIQA, SIQA, OpenbookQA, ARC-Easy/Challenge, CommonsenseQA), world knowledge (NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA), reading comprehension (BoolQ, QuAC, DROP)
  - aggregated (MMLU, HELM, BBH, AGI Eval): subparts could be done
- Status
  - 41.2% of MATH; covers static QA tests solved by 4 closed-weight + 9 open-weight SOTA models; complete metrics, few-shot prompting
  - reasoning gap 58.35% to 80.31%
  - CoT / ToT / CoC might lower it; open until 100% functionalized MATH()
  - future: GSM8K, HumanEval, MBPP

## 2.1 Contributions

- framework for models that have seen the whole internet (infinite snapshots, probabilistic newness guarantee, step-by-step derivation needed)
- functional MATH + public snapshots (code never public; three snapshots per quarter; {Oct, Nov, Dec}-2023 at https://github.com/consequentai/fneval/)
- robust to contamination (consistent across e.g. three snapshots -> proper reasoning)
- reasoning gap (gap-0 true reasoning, gap-100 full memorization; possible training objective)
- open problem: training gap-0 models

## 2.1 Contributions

This work presents the first steps towards evaluating reasoning with functional benchmarks:

- Framework for evaluation for models that have seen the text of the entire internet: We propose a long-term solution to the problem of evaluating models that are more and more trained on all written knowledge. The framework lets a benchmark be instantiated to infinite snapshots, with a probabilistic guarantee that a new snapshot did not exist before. For a static QA in the benchmark whose test captures a specific reasoning process, each snapshot QA* follows the same process, but the test is new. To do well on a set of snapshots, a model will need to do step-by-step derivations to get to an answer, instead of just recalling a static final answer.

- Functional version of MATH, an important benchmark for reasoning evaluation, and its publicly available snapshots: Our framework is designed so that existing benchmarks, which models are already tested on, can be reworked without modification. We are in the process of functionalizing the whole MATH benchmark. The specific functionalization code will never be made public. Instead three snapshots will be released every quarter. The {Oct, Nov, Dec}-2023 snapshots are available at https://github.com/consequentai/fneval/ together with the evaluation code. The repository will be kept up to date with the last quarter's snapshots.

- Robust evaluations that resist contamination: A functional benchmark has infinite snapshots, and the reasoning in each one stays identical. If a model solves a problem consistently across multiple snapshots (e.g., three snapshots), then it is highly likely that it does so with proper reasoning, because getting the answer right across many snapshots by chance should be fairly difficult.

- Reasoning gap: We define the reasoning gap as the quantitative measure of the difference in accuracy when testing against static vs functional variants. The gap measures reasoning vs memorization, where gap-0 is true reasoning and gap-100 is full memorization. The community should aim to build models with the highest accuracy while keeping the gap close to 0. Minimizing the gap may be used as a training optimization objective that could lead to models that are better at generalized reasoning.

- Open problem of training gap-0 models: We show that even the current best models have large reasoning gaps, with the caveat that the gap is likely to be smaller with more sophisticated prompting strategies. Our current datasets, training, fine-tuning, and inference strategies might be non-optimal for training gap-0 models. We leave training gap-0 models as an open problem.

steps.text:
Accurately evaluating reasoning performance is critical to improving large language models (LLMs) beyond their current capabilities. The current standard for benchmarking fails to accurately measure the reasoning of LLMs. An accurate test should pose a question whose answer can be derived under the assumption of the axioms for that domain. Reasoning systems (or humans) should be able to conclude the answer despite not having seen the question before. An ideal system would provide not only the answer but also each step of the derivation; explicit elucidation of steps is ideal, but not critical. State-of-the-art language models exhibit some reasoning capabilities, but accurate evaluation is lagging. In particular, the capabilities of LLMs may be overestimated because they are tested on benchmarks that are sufficient for language understanding (textual question, answer) but may not accurately measure reasoning.

When testing generalized problem-solving, the aim is to assess whether the system can effectively answer questions it has not encountered before. This is the opposite objective to knowledge retrieval. Finding novel questions is challenging when the model has been trained on a snapshot of the internet. Even if datasets exist that are not currently on the internet, it is unreasonable to expect them to remain so, or that we will continue to develop novel datasets. Contamination-testing by checking for k-contiguous token sequences fails to account for various other forms of leakage, especially when the benchmark is a set of static text question-answers ("static QAs"). These include i) accidental leakage from paraphrasing or compressed representations in the training data or fragments of semantically similar statements; ii) not accounting for the provenance of data used in every stage of training or fine-tuning, which becomes increasingly difficult as more models are trained from existing high-quality starting weights; iii) sourcing synthetic training data from an existing model which could be contaminated, especially if it is closed-source and closed-data, iv) overfitting through preference tuning, which may in the extreme case cause reinforcement feedback that allows the model to evolve to discover correct static answers.

Checking against a static QA is only an indirect test of reasoning. Text questions and answers work well for humans, as producing correct answers implies likely correct stepwise reasoning. The same does not apply to model outputs.

We propose an alternative approach that alleviates the concerns with static QA testing, and also works seamlessly with existing evaluation harnesses. We propose rewriting each static QA's reasoning into code, whose inputs can be varied to create infinite versions that follow the same reasoning pattern, but where the steps needed in each would be different. We call this the functional variant of the benchmark; running each of those code fragments creates a snapshot that is a drop-in replacement in the existing static evaluation harness. The accuracy on these replacements, with the static variant included, might be lower than that on the static variant alone, and we quantify this as the reasoning gap.

For domains where this can be done, using functional variants would improve on static QA evaluation. We would convert a static benchmark Bench (e.g., MATH or GSM8K or HumanEval) into its functional variant Bench(rngs). The functional variants (denoted here as QA(rngs)) take as inputs a set of deterministic typed random generators rngs, which output a pseudorandom typed value, e.g., natural int, positive or negative float, fractions, string, positive evens or odds, primes. When seeded, the rngs make the instantiation deterministic, generating a snapshot of each test (denoted here as QA*) and of the entire benchmark.

Each QA* text pair in this snapshot differs from the original static QA, but answering QA* requires the same reasoning used in the static QA. To have an unbiased accurate baseline, we created the functionalization manually by rewriting the reasoning of each test into code. Functionalization, a one-time and time-consuming task, results in infinite snapshot instantiations to test against.

Of the popular benchmarks, functionalization is easy for the subcategories of math (MATH [1] and GSM8K [2]), and code (HumanEval [3], MBPP [4], and Natural2Code [5]). The categories of commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag [6], Winogrande [7], PIQA [8], SIQA [9], OpenbookQA [10], ARC-Easy/Challenge [11], CommonsenseQA [12]), world knowledge (NaturalQuestions [13], TriviaQA [14]), and reading comprehension (BoolQ [15], QuAC [16], DROP [17]) test English understanding and so are not good candidates for functionalization. Subparts of the aggregated benchmarks (MMLU [18], HELM [19], BBH [20], and AGI Eval [21]) could be functionalized.

As of this work, we have functionalized 41.2% of the MATH benchmark, choosing the subset so as to fully cover the static QA tests solved by 4 closed-weight and 9 open-weight state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. This allows us to provide complete metrics over all of MATH for these models, assuming a simple few-shot prompting strategy. We find a reasoning gap of 58.35% to 80.31% across these models. The gap when using optimized prompting such as chain-of-thought (CoT [22]), tree-of-thought (ToT [23]), chain-of-code (CoC [24]), amongst others, could be lower, and we will resolve that open question once we have built the 100% functionalized MATH().

In future work, we will present functionalized variants of GSM8K, HumanEval, and MBPP.

## 2.1 Contributions

This work presents the first steps towards reasoning evaluation with functional benchmarks:

- Framework for evaluation for models that have seen the text of the entire internet: We present a proposal for a long-term solution to the problem of evaluating models that are increasingly trained on all written knowledge. The framework allows a benchmark to be instantiated to infinite snapshots, with a probabilistic guarantee that a new snapshot will not have existed before. For a static QA in the benchmark whose individual test captures a specific reasoning process, each snapshot QA* follows the same process, but the test is new. To perform well on a set of snapshots, a model will need to perform step-by-step derivations to reach an answer, rather than simply recalling a static final answer.

- Functional version of MATH, an important benchmark for reasoning evaluation, and its publicly available snapshots: Our framework is designed to allow reworking existing benchmarks on which models are already being tested, without modification. We are in the process of functionalizing the entire MATH benchmark. The specific functionalization code will never be publicly accessible; instead, three snapshots will be released every quarter. The {Oct, Nov, Dec}-2023 snapshots are available at https://github.com/consequentai/fneval/ along with the evaluation code. The repository will be kept up to date with the last quarter's snapshots.

- Robust evaluations that are resistant to contamination: A functional benchmark has infinite snapshots, with the reasoning involved in each remaining identical. If a model consistently solves a problem across multiple snapshots (e.g., three snapshots), there is a high likelihood that it does so with proper reasoning, as it should be fairly difficult to get the answer right across many snapshots by chance.

- Reasoning gap: We define the reasoning gap as the quantitative measure of the difference in accuracy when testing against static vs functional variants. The gap measures reasoning vs memorization, with gap-0 being true reasoning and gap-100 being full memorization. The community should aim to build models with the highest accuracy while maintaining a gap close to 0. Minimizing the gap may serve as a training optimization objective that could lead to models that perform better at generalized reasoning.

- Open problem of training gap-0 models: We show that even the current best models have large reasoning gaps, with the caveat that the gap is likely to be smaller with more sophisticated prompting strategies. Our current datasets, training, fine-tuning, and inference strategies might be non-optimal for training gap-0 models. We leave training gap-0 models as an open problem.
